title: Associations of long-term and short-term summertime temperature with survival among patients with cardiovascular disease: A UK-wide retrospective cohort study
content:
by Ka Yan Lai, Chris Webster, John Gallacher, Chinmoy Sarkar

Evidence examining the long-term and acute effects of summertime temperature on survival among patients with cardiovascular diseases (CVD) is lacking. This study examined associations of both long-term summertime temperature and heatwaves as well as short-term extreme temperature with risk of mortality in patients with CVD and its types. We identified new-onset cases of CVD and its specific types including atrial fibrillation, ischemic heart disease (IHD), heart failure and stroke from linked hospital records in the nationwide UK Biobank cohort. Annual summertime heat exposures in terms of mean temperature and annual heatwaves were measured at 1x1 Km2 spatial resolution. Daily mean temperature and temperature change between neighbouring days (TCN) were measured over lag 0–5 days. Cox proportional hazard model was used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) for long-term associations. We used individual-level time stratified case-crossover design to examine short-term associations of mean daily summertime temperature and TCN with mortality. We identified 63,860 patients with new-onset CVD, of which 12,237 (19.2%) died with mean follow-up of 6.1 years. Each 1°C increment in annual mean summertime temperature was associated with 15% higher risk of mortality for CVD patients (HR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.24), 10% for atrial fibrillation (1.10; 1.00-1.21), and 19% for IHD (1.19; 1.07-1.33). Risks of mortality remained significantly higher in the group exposed to highest number of annual heatwaves in patients with CVD, and for atrial fibrillation, and heart failure. We identified higher risks of mortality associated with increased summertime temperature in patients of low/moderate (compared with high) education attainment, residing in deprived areas and in neighbourhoods with moderate (compared with high) residential greenspace coverage, suggesting the importance of community planning in climate resilience. Consistently, short-term acute exposure to high temperature was associated with higher risks of mortality for the patient subgroups (OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.23-2.34 for CVD; OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42 for atrial fibrillation and OR, 1.67; 95% CI, 1.04-2.67 for IHD). Similarly, positive TCN was associated with higher odds of mortality among patients with CVD, IHD and heart failure as compared with 0 °C temperature change. Our study found that exposure to extreme summertime temperature is a risk factor for mortality among CVD patients. Planning an appropriate mix of community-based strategies together with personalized adaptations for reducing sensitivity to extreme temperature will constitute vital preventive interventions.
